# The "Learning" Intuition {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #00C9A7)"}

Teaching the model to write its own function.

## Recap: Traditional vs. Machine Learning

In **Part 1**, we saw that Machine Learning flips the paradigm. Instead of writing the logic, we let the data "train" the function.

```{dot}
//| echo: false
//| fig-width: 10
//| fig-height: 4.2
digraph concept {
    graph [rankdir=LR fontname="Helvetica" nodesep=0.4 ranksep=1.5]
    node  [fontname="Helvetica" fontcolor=white style=filled shape=box penwidth=0 margin="0.25,0.15" fontsize=13]
    edge  [penwidth=2.5 arrowsize=1.0 fontname="Helvetica" fontsize=12]

    // ── Traditional row ──
    subgraph cluster_trad {
        label="Traditional Programming" fontcolor="#8899bb" fontsize=13 style=dashed color="#3A5070" margin=18
        ti [label="Input" fillcolor="#2D4E7E"]
        tf [label="f(x)\nyou write it" fillcolor="#4a4a6a"]
        to [label="Output" fillcolor="#2D4E7E"]
        ti -> tf [color="#8899bb"]
        tf -> to [color="#8899bb"]
    }

    // ── Machine Learning row ──
    subgraph cluster_ml {
        label="Machine Learning" fontcolor="#00C9A7" fontsize=13 style=dashed color="#00C9A7" margin=18
        mi   [label="Input" fillcolor="#2D4E7E"]
        mf   [label="f(x)\nlearned from data" fillcolor="#00C9A7" fontcolor="#1C355E" fontname="Helvetica-Bold"]
        mo   [label="Output" fillcolor="#2D4E7E"]
        data [label="Data" fillcolor="#1a4060" shape=cylinder]
        { rank=same; mf; data }
        mi   -> mf [color="#00C9A7"]
        mf   -> mo [color="#00C9A7"]
        data -> mf [label="trains" color="#5599aa" style=dashed fontcolor="#5599aa" fontsize=11]
    }
}
```

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
**Goal:** We provide **Input** (Images) and **Ground Truth** (Labels). The model adjusts itself until its **Output** matches the Ground Truth.
:::

## The Feedback Loop: How a Model Learns

Learning is a cycle of making a guess, seeing how wrong it is, and adjusting.

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
1. **Predict:** Model guesses where the objects are.
2. **Compare:** We compare the guess to the **Ground Truth** labels.
3. **Loss:** We calculate a "Loss" score (how wrong the guess was).
4. **Update:** We adjust the model's weights to make the loss smaller next time.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" .fragment}
This cycle repeats thousands of times over **Epochs** (one pass through the full dataset).
:::

# Why We Need "Loss" {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #00C9A7)"}

The math that drives the learning.

## Business Metrics vs. Training Loss

In **Part 3**, we used metrics like **mAP, Precision, and Recall**. Why can't the model just use those to learn?

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
**The Problem:** Business metrics are **"jumpy"** (discrete). 
- If a bounding box moves 1 pixel, the IoU might drop from 0.51 to 0.49.
- Suddenly, a "Success" becomes a "Failure."
- This "cliff" makes it impossible for the model to know which way to improve.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
**The Solution:** We need a **"Smooth" Metric** (Loss Function) that gives a gradient—telling the model exactly how much better or worse it's getting with every tiny adjustment.
:::

## What is a Loss Function?

> A **single number** that measures how wrong the model's prediction is — the lower, the better.

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
``` {=html}
<div style="display:flex; align-items:stretch; gap:1.2rem; margin-top:1rem; font-size:0.88em; justify-content:center;">
  <div style="background:rgba(28,53,94,0.08); border-radius:10px; padding:0.8rem 1.2rem; text-align:center; min-width:140px;">
    🧠 <strong>Prediction</strong><br>
    <span style="color:#64748b; font-size:0.82em;">model output</span>
  </div>
  <div style="display:flex; align-items:center; font-size:1.3rem; color:#94a3b8;">→</div>
  <div style="background:rgba(220,53,69,0.10); border:2px dashed #dc3545; border-radius:10px; padding:0.8rem 1.2rem; text-align:center; min-width:160px;">
    ⚖️ <strong>Loss Function</strong><br>
    <span style="color:#dc3545; font-size:0.82em;">measures the gap</span>
  </div>
  <div style="display:flex; align-items:center; font-size:1.3rem; color:#94a3b8;">→</div>
  <div style="background:rgba(0,201,167,0.10); border-radius:10px; padding:0.8rem 1.2rem; text-align:center; min-width:140px;">
    🔧 <strong>Weight Update</strong><br>
    <span style="color:#00C9A7; font-size:0.82em;">model improves</span>
  </div>
</div>
```
:::

## MSE — The Most Intuitive Loss

**Mean Squared Error** is the simplest, most widely used loss in machine learning.

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(y_i - \hat{y}_i\bigr)^2$$

| Symbol | Meaning |
|:---:|:---|
| $y_i$ | Ground-truth value (the label) |
| $\hat{y}_i$ | Model's predicted value |
| $(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2$ | Squared error — big mistakes hurt **much more** |
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal" .fragment .fade-up}
Each task eventually gets a better-tuned loss (cross-entropy for classes, IoU-based for boxes) — but **MSE is the intuition** behind all of them.
:::

## Following the Gradient

> How does the model actually use the loss to improve?

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
It finds the **direction that decreases the loss the fastest** — the gradient — and takes a small step that way. This is called **gradient descent**.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
```{=html}
<iframe src="assets/html/demo_gradient_descent.html"
        width="100%" height="370px"
        style="border:none; border-radius:12px; overflow:hidden;"
        scrolling="no">
</iframe>
```
:::

## YOLO's Loss: Three Signals

YOLO's training loss is the **sum of three components**, each measuring a different type of mistake:

::: {.fragment .fade-up style="margin-top: 0.5rem;"}
| Component | Also called | What it penalizes |
|:---|:---:|:---|
| **Box Loss** | `box_loss` | Wrong bounding-box coordinates (position & size) |
| **Class Loss** | `cls_loss` | Wrong class label (Car vs. Truck vs. Person) |
| **Distribution Focal Loss** | `dfl_loss` | Imprecise box boundary distributions |
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up style="margin-top: 1rem;"}
$$\mathcal{L}_{total} = \lambda_{box}\,\mathcal{L}_{box} + \lambda_{cls}\,\mathcal{L}_{cls} + \lambda_{dfl}\,\mathcal{L}_{dfl}$$
:::

# Diagnosing Training {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #00C9A7)"}

Reading the curves to fix what training isn't learning.

## The Training Spectrum

*Every training run lands somewhere on this spectrum — knowing where is the first step to fixing it.*

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="33%"}

::: {.callout-warning}
### 🔴 Overfitting
Model **memorizes** training data.

- Train mAP >> Val mAP
- Val loss starts rising

**Too much capacity for your data**
:::

:::

::: {.column width="34%"}

::: {.callout-tip}
### 🟢 Just Right
Model **generalizes** to new data.

- Train ≈ Val, both high
- Both losses converge low

**The goal — stay here**
:::

:::

::: {.column width="33%"}

::: {.callout-note}
### 🟠 Underfitting
Model **never learned** the patterns.

- Both Train and Val mAP low
- Losses barely decrease

**Too little capacity or training**
:::

:::

::::

## 🔴 Overfitting: The Symptom

> The model memorizes training data instead of learning general patterns.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="42%"}

**What you see:**

- Train loss ↓, Val loss ↑
- Train mAP climbs, Val mAP stalls
- Growing gap between the two curves

:::

::: {.column width="58%"}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

np.random.seed(7)
epochs = np.arange(1, 31)
train_loss = 0.5 * np.exp(-epochs/10) + 0.02 * np.random.rand(30)
val_loss = 0.6 * np.exp(-epochs/8) + 0.02 * np.random.rand(30)
val_loss[12:] = val_loss[12:] + 0.022 * np.arange(1, 19)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
fig.patch.set_alpha(0.0)
ax.patch.set_alpha(0.0)

ax.plot(epochs, train_loss, color='#1C355E', linewidth=3, label='Train Loss')
ax.plot(epochs, val_loss, color='#00C9A7', linewidth=3, label='Val Loss')
ax.axvline(x=13, color='#dc3545', linewidth=1.5, linestyle='--', alpha=0.7)
ax.annotate('Val loss starts rising', xy=(13, val_loss[12]), xytext=(16, 0.65),
            fontsize=9, color='#dc3545',
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color='#dc3545', lw=1.2))

ax.set_xlabel('Epochs', fontsize=12, color='#1C355E')
ax.set_ylabel('Loss', fontsize=12, color='#1C355E')
ax.set_title('Overfitting: Diverging Losses', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold', color='#1C355E')
ax.legend(frameon=False)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.0)
ax.set_yticks(np.arange(0, 1.1, 0.1))
ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False)
ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
ax.spines['bottom'].set_color('#1C355E')
ax.spines['left'].set_color('#1C355E')
ax.tick_params(colors='#1C355E')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

::::

## 🟠 Underfitting: The Symptom

> The model hasn't learned the patterns — too simple, over-constrained, or undertrained.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="45%"}

**What you see:**

- Both Train *and* Val mAP **low and flat**
- Loss barely moves after the first epochs
- Curves close together — but both stuck high

:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

np.random.seed(3)
epochs = np.arange(1, 31)
train_loss = 0.4 + 0.2 * np.exp(-epochs/5) + 0.02 * np.random.rand(30)
val_loss = 0.45 + 0.2 * np.exp(-epochs/5) + 0.02 * np.random.rand(30)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
fig.patch.set_alpha(0.0)
ax.patch.set_alpha(0.0)

ax.plot(epochs, train_loss, color='#1C355E', linewidth=3, label='Train Loss')
ax.plot(epochs, val_loss, color='#00C9A7', linewidth=3, label='Val Loss')
ax.annotate('Both stuck — barely dropping', xy=(20, train_loss[19]),
            xytext=(12, 0.75), fontsize=9, color='#E07B39',
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color='#E07B39', lw=1.2))

ax.set_xlabel('Epochs', fontsize=12, color='#1C355E')
ax.set_ylabel('Loss', fontsize=12, color='#1C355E')
ax.set_title('Underfitting: High Plateau', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold', color='#1C355E')
ax.legend(frameon=False)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.0)
ax.set_yticks(np.arange(0, 1.1, 0.1))
ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False)
ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
ax.spines['bottom'].set_color('#1C355E')
ax.spines['left'].set_color('#1C355E')
ax.tick_params(colors='#1C355E')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

::::

## Diagnosing Your Training Run

*Use this as a reference when reading your own loss curves.*

| What you see | Problem | Actions |
|:---|:---:|:---|
| Train mAP >> Val mAP, Val loss rising | 🔴 **Overfitting** | Add augmentation · increase `weight_decay` · set `patience` |
| Both mAP low and flat, loss barely moves | 🟠 **Underfitting** | Bigger model · more `epochs` · raise `lr0` · lower `weight_decay` |
| Both losses converging, mAP climbing | 🟢 **Healthy** | Continue training or deploy |

::: {.callout-tip}
**Always watch both curves.** 99% train accuracy means nothing if val is failing.
:::

# Practical Data Pipeline {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #00C9A7)"}

Formatting and fixing your data for YOLO.

## What If Your Metrics Reveal a Problem?

You can now read your validation results — but what do you do when the numbers look bad?

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
The most common culprits are:

- **Class imbalance** — rare classes get ignored during training
- **Overfitting or underfitting** — the model hasn't generalized
- **Poor hyperparameters** — learning rate, weight decay, stopping too early or too late
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
We'll fix the **data-side** problem here (imbalance). The training-side fixes (augmentation, hyperparameters) come next.
:::

## Class Imbalance: Fixing the Bias

How do we stop the model from ignoring rare classes during training?

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.5))
fig.patch.set_alpha(0.0)

brand_dark = '#1C355E'
brand_teal = '#00C9A7'
brand_red  = '#dc3545'

classes = ['Empty Spot', 'Car']

for ax in axes:
    ax.patch.set_alpha(0.0)
    ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False)
    ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
    ax.spines['bottom'].set_color(brand_dark)
    ax.spines['left'].set_color(brand_dark)
    ax.tick_params(colors=brand_dark, labelsize=11)

# Before: imbalanced
counts_before = [9500, 500]
colors_before = [brand_dark, brand_red]
axes[0].bar(classes, counts_before, color=colors_before, alpha=0.85, width=0.5)
axes[0].set_title('Before: Imbalanced', fontsize=13, fontweight='bold', color=brand_dark)
axes[0].set_ylabel('Training samples', fontsize=11, color=brand_dark)
for i, v in enumerate(counts_before):
    axes[0].text(i, v + 100, str(v), ha='center', fontsize=12, fontweight='bold', color=brand_dark)
axes[0].set_ylim(0, 11000)

# After: balanced via weighted sampling
counts_after = [9500, 9500]
colors_after = [brand_teal, brand_teal]
axes[1].bar(classes, counts_after, color=colors_after, alpha=0.85, width=0.5)
axes[1].set_title('After: Weighted Sampling', fontsize=13, fontweight='bold', color=brand_dark)
for i, v in enumerate(counts_after):
    axes[1].text(i, v + 100, str(v), ha='center', fontsize=12, fontweight='bold', color=brand_dark)
axes[1].set_ylim(0, 11000)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Here we oversample (duplicating images) the minority class (car) to make it learnable.

## Understanding the Data Setup

Different formats for different tasks:

- **Classification**: Relies *entirely* on folder structure (e.g., `train/cat/`, `train/dog/`).
- **Detection & Segmentation**: Uses standard **YOLO format**, pairing images with `.txt` label files.

```text
my_dataset/
├── images/
│   ├── train/
│   └── val/
└── labels/
    ├── train/
    └── val/
```

## Inside the Labels

- **Object Detection** (`.txt` Bounding Box):
  `<class_index> <x_center> <y_center> <width> <height>`

- **Instance Segmentation** (`.txt` Polygon):
  `<class_index> <x1> <y1> <x2> <y2> ... <xn> <yn>`

**⚠ Note:** Coordinates must **always be normalized** (0.0 to 1.0) to keep annotations independent of image resolution!

## The `data.yaml` File

Linking indices to names and defining paths.

```yaml
# data.yaml
path: ../my_dataset
train: images/train
val: images/val

names:
  0: my_custom_object
  1: another_object
```

## Data Leakage: The Silent Killer

**The Problem:** Validation/test data accidentally ends up in the training set.

**The Danger:** Val metrics look "perfect," but the model fails in production.

**How to Avoid:**
- Use `autosplit()` for automatic, safe partitioning.
- Avoid manually copying images between split folders.
- Check for duplicates/hashes before training.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Suspiciously perfect metrics? Check for leakage!**
:::

## Labeling Your Own Data

Typing coordinates manually is impossible. Use **Ultralytics HUB**, Roboflow, or CVAT.

1. Upload your images.
2. Draw bounding boxes or polygons visually.
3. Export in **YOLO format** for a ready-to-train dataset structure!

*Docs Reference: [Ultralytics HUB](https://docs.ultralytics.com/hub/)*

## AutoLabeling with SAM

Speed up labeling using **SAM** (Segment Anything Model):

1. **Zero-Shot Labeling:** Bypass manual labeling for generic objects.
2. Run SAM on your raw dataset to generate masks/boxes.
3. Review and correct the auto-generated labels—drastically faster than drawing manually!

*Docs Reference: [Segment Anything Models (SAM)](https://docs.ultralytics.com/models/sam/)*

# Kickoff Training {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #00C9A7)"}

Hyperparameters and Configs.

## Training

We can start training directly from the command line or Python API:

```bash
yolo train model=weights/yolo26n.pt data=data.yaml epochs=100 imgsz=640 batch=-1
```

```python
# Python Equivalent
from ultralytics import YOLO

model = YOLO("weights/yolo26n.pt")
results = model.train(data="data.yaml", epochs=100, imgsz=640, batch=-1)
```

## Transfer Learning

- **`.pt` (Pretrained weights):** Starts with general features (edges, shapes) from large datasets. Fast training, needs little data. (*Always recommended!*)
- **`.yaml` (Architecture Definition):** Blank blueprint. Random weights, meaning you train entirely from scratch.

*Use a `.pt` model for all custom dataset training to leverage Transfer Learning.*

## Important Hyperparameters

- `epochs` (Default: 100): Pass through the ENTIRE dataset. More = learns more, but risks overfitting.
- `batch` (Default: 16): Images processed at once.
  - Higher = faster, stable, takes more GPU memory.
  - Smaller = adds noise, longer training.
  - *Pro-tip*: Use `batch: -1` for **AutoBatch** to maximize your GPU memory!
- `imgsz` (Default: 640): Target image size. Larger sizes (e.g., 1024) capture more detail but use more RAM.

## Hyperparameters: Tuning the Steps

- **Learning Rate (`lr0`)**: Controls step size—too large and the ball overshoots, too small and training is slow.
- **Weight Decay**: Penalizes large weights to prevent memorization (🔴 Overfitting).
- **Patience (`early_stopping`)**: Stop training if validation metrics haven't improved for $N$ epochs.

## 💡 Tip for Tiny Objects: SAHI

**Problem:** A 4K image resized to 640px makes tiny objects *invisible* to YOLO.

**Solution — [SAHI](https://docs.ultralytics.com/guides/sahi-tiled-inference/):**
1. **Slice** the large image into small, overlapping tiles.
2. **Run YOLO** on each tile at full resolution.
3. **Merge** all detections back together automatically.

## Data Augmentation (Albumentations)

YOLO natively supports **Albumentations** to improve model robustness:

```python
import albumentations as A
from ultralytics import YOLO

model = YOLO("yolo26n.pt")

# Define custom transforms
custom_transforms = [
    A.Blur(blur_limit=7, p=0.5),
    A.HorizontalFlip(p=0.5),
    A.RandomBrightnessContrast(p=0.5),
]

# Train the model with custom transforms
model.train(data="data.yaml", epochs=100, augmentations=custom_transforms)
```
